analysis.one_liner: Expanded foreign electronic surveillance and barred lawsuits against phone companies that helped spy.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 64 Republican cosponsors but never got a House vote; a discharge petition to force it out of committee fell short, and it died when the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let the Attorney General and the Director of National Intelligence authorize, for up to a year at a time, the surveillance of people overseas to collect foreign intelligence — without a court order for each target. Phone and internet companies would be legally required to help, would be paid for it, and would be shielded from lawsuits for doing so. It would also bar civil suits against companies for surveillance assistance they already provided, and stop states from investigating or suing them over it.
analysis.who_benefits: Telephone and internet companies gain the most: the bill blocks any lawsuit against them for helping the government spy, and stops state investigations into that conduct. The executive branch gains authority to run year-long surveillance programs targeting people abroad with court review of its written procedures rather than of each target. The providers are compensated at the prevailing rate for their assistance.

how_it_helps.text: Lets the Attorney General and Director of National Intelligence jointly authorize, for periods up to one year, surveillance of people reasonably believed to be outside the United States, without an individual court order for each target [S2].

Prohibits civil lawsuits against any communication service provider that furnished surveillance assistance requested by the intelligence community, and bars states from investigating, sanctioning, or suing such providers [S2].

Requires companies to immediately provide the government all information, facilities, and assistance needed for an acquisition, while compensating them at the prevailing rate and freeing them from liability for complying [S3].

Adds authority to acquire foreign intelligence to prevent the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, and lets the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court sit as a full panel on questions of exceptional importance [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary Americans lose privacy protections. Their international communications can be collected under program-level authorizations rather than individual court orders, and the court reviews the government's written procedures rather than specific targets. People who believed their rights were violated lose the ability to sue the companies involved, and the emergency window for certain surveillance without a court order doubles from 48 hours to seven days.
analysis.who_pays_short: Americans' privacy and access to courts

drawbacks.text: The bill allows the government to sweep in Americans' communications without a judge ever reviewing an individual target — surveillance of non-citizens abroad needs only the Attorney General and DNI's joint certification, with the court checking procedures, not specific interceptions [S2].
Its immunity provisions would erase pending lawsuits over companies' past cooperation with warrantless surveillance and preempt state investigations and enforcement against those providers [S2].
It extends the time the Attorney General can run emergency pen registers and trap-and-trace devices before seeking a court order from 48 hours to seven days [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's defenders could argue it closes intelligence gaps on targets overseas and gives companies clear legal cover. But its cost falls almost entirely on ordinary Americans: surveillance of international calls and emails would run on program-level certifications instead of individual court orders, and anyone whose rights were violated would lose their day in court because the companies involved would be immune. Notably, while this particular bill died, Congress passed a nearly identical framework later in 2008 — the FISA Amendments Act that became law in July — with the telecom immunity included, so the substance advanced regardless of this bill's fate.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary and Intelligence committees, sent to a crime subcommittee, and never got a hearing or floor vote; the sponsor's discharge petition — a procedural move to pull a bill out of committee if a majority of the House signs — did not succeed, and the bill died when the 110th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 14, 2008 by Rep. Vito Fossella and referred to the House Judiciary Committee and the Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence [S1].
On March 17, 2008 it was referred to the Judiciary Committee's Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security, where it received no further action [S5].
On April 23, 2008, Fossella filed a discharge petition (Petition No. 110-7) to try to force the bill out of committee and onto the floor [S5].
The bill had 64 cosponsors, all Republicans [S4].
No further action was taken before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, and the bill expired without a vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Telecommunications companies and the intelligence agencies came out ahead. Even though this bill died, Congress passed an essentially identical FISA expansion with telecom immunity later in 2008, which was signed into law in July — so the bill's chief beneficiaries got what they wanted by another route.

for.name: Rep. Vito Fossella
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and filed a discharge petition on April 23, 2008 to try to force it to the House floor.

for.name: President George W. Bush
for.what_they_did: Publicly pressed Congress during the 2008 FISA debate to grant telecommunications companies retroactive immunity for assisting government surveillance.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security subcommittee on March 17, 2008 and held no markup or floor action on it.

against.name: House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence
against.what_they_did: Received the referral but took no recorded action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All 64 cosponsors were Republicans and the bill never reached a floor vote, so there is no recorded division — support was entirely one-party, and the bill stalled in committee without any vote at all.

industries.note: The bill would force these companies to assist government surveillance, pay them for it, and — most importantly — bar all civil lawsuits and state investigations against them for that assistance, including assistance already given. Their gain comes directly at the expense of Americans' ability to hold the companies accountable in court.
